texto.t: The Café That Never Throws Food Away
p: When Marta Silva opened her café in Porto five years ago, she noticed something that worried her. Every evening, her staff threw away bags of bread, cakes and salads that nobody had bought.

"It felt wrong," she says. "People in our own neighbourhood were going hungry, and we were filling bins." So Marta decided to change the way her café worked. Now, any food that hasn't been sold by six o'clock is offered at half price. Anything left after closing time is collected by a local charity, which shares it with families who need it.

At first, some customers were suspicious. "They thought half-price food meant old food," Marta explains. "But it's exactly the same food that was on the shelf that morning." Today, many people come in especially at six, and the café has become busier than ever.

The idea has spread. Three other cafés in the same street have started similar schemes, and the city council is planning to support businesses that reduce waste. Marta, however, says the most important change is personal: "I sleep better now. Nothing we make is wasted."

q.q: What worried Marta when she opened the café?
o: The amount of food that was thrown away.

q.q: What happens to food that hasn't been sold by six?
o: It is given to the staff.

q.q: Who receives the food left after closing time?
Why were some customers suspicious at first?
o: They thought the cheaper food was old.
They thought the prices were too high.

q.q: What does Marta say is the most important change?
o: She feels better about her work.

texto.t: Why Boredom Might Be Good for You
p: Most of us go to great lengths to avoid being bored. We check our phones in queues, listen to podcasts while cooking and fill every quiet moment with something to watch. Yet a growing number of psychologists argue that boredom, far from being a waste of time, may serve a useful purpose.

In one well-known experiment, participants were first given a deliberately dull task: copying numbers from a phone directory. Afterwards, they were asked to think of as many uses as possible for a pair of plastic cups. Those who had done the boring task came up with more ideas, and more original ones, than a group who had skipped it. The researchers concluded that boredom pushes the mind to wander, and that a wandering mind tends to make unexpected connections.

This does not mean that all boredom is beneficial. When people feel trapped in a situation they cannot change, such as a repetitive job with no prospects, boredom is linked to stress and poor health rather than creativity. The key difference seems to be whether we have the freedom to let our thoughts drift.

Some schools have begun to take these findings seriously. Rather than filling every minute of the day with activities, teachers are building in short periods of unstructured time. Early reports suggest that children use these moments to invent games and stories, although critics point out that it is too soon to measure any long-term effect.
For adults, the advice is simple, if not always easy to follow: next time you are waiting for a bus, try leaving your phone in your pocket.

q.q: According to the first paragraph, what do most people do?
o: They try hard not to feel bored.
They spend less time on their phones.

q.q: What did the experiment show?
o: People who had been bored had more creative ideas.
Plastic cups make people more creative.

q.q: When is boredom linked to poor health?
o: When people feel they cannot escape a situation.
When people have too much free time.
When people use their phones too much.

q.q: What do critics say about the school programmes?
o: It is too early to know the long-term results.

q.q: What is the writer's final advice?
o: Allow yourself to be bored sometimes.
Listen to podcasts while you wait.

lines: Welcome back. Today I'm talking to Jin Park, who has been working from home for three years. Jin, has it been a positive experience?
Mostly, yes. I save almost two hours a day that I used to spend commuting, and I'm far more productive in the mornings.
Definitely. The biggest one is that it's hard to switch off. When your office is in your living room, work never really ends.
How do you deal with that?
I've set myself strict rules. I shut the laptop at six, and then I go for a walk, which tricks my brain into thinking I've come home.
Some managers say remote workers are less creative. Would you agree?
I'd say it depends. Formal meetings work fine online, but you lose those random conversations by the coffee machine, which is where a lot of good ideas come from.
So what would your ideal arrangement be?
Probably two days in the office and three at home. That way I'd get the best of both worlds.

o: He no longer spends time commuting.

q.q: What does Jin find most difficult?
o: Stopping work at the end of the day.

o: To feel as if he has come home from work.

q.q: What does Jin say about creativity?
o: Informal chats in the office are hard to replace.

Online meetings produce the best ideas.

q.q: What would Jin prefer?

tarefa.pedido: Escreva um ensaio sobre a frase: “Todo jovem deveria fazer um ano de trabalho voluntário antes da faculdade.” Apresente argumentos dos dois lados e termine com a sua opinião. Entre 140 e 190 palavras.
precisa: o outro lado (However / On the other hand)
\b(in conclusion|to sum up|overall|all things considered|to conclude)\b
evitar: Em texto formal, evite gonna, wanna e gotta.
tarefa.modelo:
Many people believe that a year of volunteer work would help young people before they start university. In my view, this idea has clear benefits, although it should not be compulsory.
On the one hand, volunteering teaches skills that are rarely learned at school. For example, a student who helps in a hospital or an environmental project learns to work in a team, solve real problems and deal with responsibility. Furthermore, many young people are not sure what they want to study, and a year away from books can help them make a better choice.
On the other hand, not every family can afford to support a child who is neither earning nor studying. Moreover, some students are highly motivated and would simply lose a year. However, these problems could be reduced if volunteers received a small allowance.
In conclusion, I believe a volunteer year is valuable and should be encouraged with financial support, but students should be free to decide for themselves.

tarefa.pergunta: Some people say social media does more harm than good. What do you think?

precisa: o outro lado (on the other hand / however)
uma ressalva (it depends / to some extent)
tarefa.modelo: I'd say it depends on how you use it. On the one hand, social media helps people stay in touch: for example, I talk to my cousins in Canada every week. On the other hand, it can be addictive, and some studies suggest that teenagers who spend hours online tend to feel more anxious. Personally, I think the problem isn't the technology itself, but the lack of limits.

texto.t: The Overlooked Value of Weak Ties
p: When we think about the people who shape our lives, we tend to picture close friends and family. Yet an influential line of sociological research suggests that some of the most consequential connections are those we barely think about: acquaintances, former colleagues, the friend of a friend we chat to at parties.

In a classic study of job seekers, researchers found that people were more likely to have found their current job through an acquaintance than through a close friend. The reasoning is elegant. Our close friends tend to move in the same circles as we do, so they largely know what we already know. Acquaintances, by contrast, connect us to different networks, and therefore to information we would not otherwise encounter.

More recent research using data from professional networking sites has added nuance to this picture. It was not the very weakest ties that proved most useful, but moderately weak ones: people with whom one shares a few mutual contacts, but not many. Ties that were too distant offered little trust; those that were too close offered little new information.

The implications extend beyond careers. Brief, friendly interactions with acquaintances, such as a chat with a neighbour or a regular at the café, appear to contribute measurably to people's sense of wellbeing and belonging. Paradoxically, these interactions are precisely the ones that tend to disappear when people work remotely or move frequently.

None of this diminishes the importance of close relationships, which provide support that acquaintances cannot. But it does suggest that a healthy social life may depend not only on the depth of our friendships, but also on their breadth.

q.q: What is the main argument of the text?
o: Acquaintances can be surprisingly important in our lives.
Close friends are less important than we think.

q.q: Why are acquaintances useful when looking for a job, according to the study?
o: They connect us to networks and information we don't already have.
They are more willing to help than friends.
They usually work in the same company.

q.q: What did the more recent research add?
o: Moderately weak ties were more useful than the very weakest ones.

q.q: What does the writer imply about remote work?
o: It may reduce the casual contacts that support wellbeing.
It improves people's sense of belonging.

q.q: What is the writer's final position?
o: Both deep and broad social connections matter.

partes.instr: Ouça um trecho de um programa de rádio sobre o sono. Você pode ouvir duas vezes.
lines: With me is Jin, who has spent the last year researching a book on sleep. Jin, is it true that we're sleeping less than previous generations?

That's the common assumption, but the evidence is surprisingly mixed. Some studies suggest average sleep has barely changed in decades. What does seem to have changed is how irregular our sleep has become, and how many of us look at screens right up until we close our eyes.
Does irregularity matter as much as the total amount?

Increasingly, researchers think it might. Going to bed at very different times disrupts the body clock, rather like having mild jet lag every Monday. Some recent work links irregular sleep to poorer mood and concentration, even when people sleep the recommended number of hours.
So what would you advise listeners to do?

Rather than obsessing over eight hours, aim for consistency: a similar wake-up time every day, including weekends. Get daylight in the morning. And treat sleep trackers with some caution. For anxious sleepers, constantly checking the data can actually make sleep worse.

q.q: What does Jin say about the idea that we sleep less than before?
o: We sleep much more than before.

q.q: What has clearly changed, according to Jin?
o: How irregular our sleep has become.
The number of hours people need.
The age at which people sleep less.

q.q: Why does Jin compare irregular sleep to jet lag?
What is Jin's main advice?
o: Keep a consistent wake-up time, even at weekends.
Check a sleep tracker every night.

q.q: What does he say about sleep trackers?
o: They can make anxious people sleep worse.

tarefa.pedido: Escreva um ensaio respondendo: “As cidades deveriam proibir os carros no centro?” Discuta duas consequências, considere o outro lado e conclua com a sua posição. Entre 180 e 220 palavras.
precisa: \b(in my view|i would argue|i believe|it could be argued)\b
a sua posição (In my view / I would argue)
evitar: Num ensaio C1, evite gonna, wanna, stuff e kinda.
Num ensaio formal, prefira as formas completas: I am, do not, cannot.
tarefa.modelo:
In recent years, a growing number of cities have experimented with restricting cars in their historic centres. In my view, such measures are largely beneficial, provided that they are introduced with care.
The first consequence is a marked improvement in air quality and safety. Fewer vehicles mean less pollution and fewer accidents, and streets that were once dominated by traffic can be reclaimed for walking, cycling and social life. Furthermore, several cities have reported that local shops benefit, as pedestrians tend to linger and return more often than drivers.
A second consequence concerns accessibility. Admittedly, a ban could make the centre harder to reach for elderly or disabled residents, as well as for workers who live in areas poorly served by public transport. Consequently, any restriction must be accompanied by reliable buses, adequate parking on the edge of the zone and exemptions for those with genuine needs.
On the other hand, it could be argued that each city is different, and that a policy which succeeds in a compact town may fail in a sprawling metropolis built around the car.
On balance, I would argue that the benefits clearly outweigh the drawbacks, as long as cities treat the transition as a gradual process rather than an overnight ban.

tarefa.pergunta: Some people say that technology has made us worse at remembering things. To what extent do you agree?
tarefa.pedido: Responda com nuance: concorde em parte, dê um exemplo, considere o outro lado e conclua.
precisa: \b(to some extent|up to a point|i'?d argue|it depends|i partly agree)\b
uma posição com nuance (To some extent...)
\b(on the other hand|however|that said|having said that|admittedly)\b
o outro lado (That said / On the other hand)
tarefa.modelo: I'd agree to some extent. For instance, I no longer remember phone numbers or directions, because my phone does it for me, and I suspect most people are the same. That said, I'm not convinced our memory is actually worse. It may simply be that we choose what to remember more strategically, and use the freed-up attention for other things. Having said that, I do think constant notifications make it harder to concentrate long enough to remember things properly. So, on balance, technology hasn't damaged our memory itself, but it has changed the habits that help us use it well.
